title: Communion for children (1905–1910)
hookLine: Pius X encourages frequent communion and first communion around age seven

lines: A ROW OF CHILDREN IN THE AISLE.
A DAY THAT USED TO COME LATER.
cards: A white dress, or a small suit and tie. A row of children walking up the aisle, hands folded, trying not to giggle. Grandparents with cameras in the pews.
In a Catholic parish, first communion is a big day, and it comes when a child is still small. That timing has a history.

Before it changed, children were often kept waiting longer, and adults who did go to communion might go only rarely, out of a sense that they were never worthy enough. A pope named Pius X set out to change both habits.

teach.b: Two documents did the work. First, the hesitation. A strict mood in parts of the Church had taught people to keep their distance from the altar, as if communion were a prize for the nearly perfect.
Second, the invitation to adults. A decree under Pius X said communion could be received often, even daily, by anyone in a state of grace who comes with a right intention.

teach.h: HELP FOR THE WEAK, NOT A PRIZE.
teach.b: Communion was described not as a reward for the holy but as help for the weak. Come often. Third, the children.
A second decree, known by its opening Latin words, Quam singulari, took up the age of first communion.
It said the age of discretion is when a child begins to reason, about the seventh year, more or less, and that children should not be kept waiting long past it.
A child didn't need to understand everything a theologian knows.
They needed to know, in their own way, that this bread is not ordinary bread, and to want it. Fourth, the root.
The decrees leaned on Jesus's words in John's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "Except you eat the flesh of the Son of man, and drink his blood, you shall not have life in you."
If the bread is life, the reasoning went, why make the hungry wait? The small children walking up the aisle today follow a path opened by two documents from one pope.

how: In the Latin Church, Catholic children usually prepare for first communion at around seven or eight, often in a parish class, after a first confession; adults who are in a state of grace may receive communion at any Mass, even daily.

practice: Think back to your first communion, if you made one: the clothes, the church, who was there. If you didn't, remember a first time at any table that mattered, a meal where you were welcomed, and notice who brought you there.
If you pray, thank God for that person by name; if not, hold them with gratitude.
